question: A pair of fair \(6\)-sided dice is rolled \(n\) times. What is the least value of \(n\) such that the probability that the sum of the numbers face up on a roll equals \(7\) at least once is greater than \(\dfrac{1}{2}?\)
solution:
It is easier to calculate the probability of never getting a sum of \(7\), because “at least once” includes many different possibilities.

On one roll, the two dice have \(6\cdot6=36\) equally likely ordered outcomes. For each of the six possible numbers on the first die, exactly one number on the second die makes the sum \(7\). Thus
\[
P(\text{sum is }7)=\frac6{36}=\frac16,
\qquad
P(\text{sum is not }7)=\frac56.
\]
The rolls are independent, so the probability of avoiding a sum of \(7\) on all \(n\) rolls is \((5/6)^n\). Therefore,
\[
P(\text{at least one sum of }7)=1-\left(\frac56\right)^n.
\]
We need this probability to be strictly greater than \(1/2\), which means
\[
\left(\frac56\right)^n<\frac12.
\]
For three rolls,
\[
\left(\frac56\right)^3=\frac{125}{216}>\frac{108}{216}=\frac12.
\]
For four rolls,
\[
\left(\frac56\right)^4=\frac{625}{1296}<\frac{648}{1296}=\frac12.
\]
Each additional roll multiplies the probability of avoiding \(7\) by \(5/6\), making it smaller. Since three rolls are insufficient and four suffice, the least value is \(\boxed{4}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
